title: Three regional emergency departments: frequent attender case management, single-site decision withdrawn for a multi-site case-control design
notes: Expert level 5 path with two decisions where the second withdraws the first, and dependency closure across Protocol and Stats in a multi-site design. The need names a matched case-control study and no other design, so classifyFamily routes it to "case-control"; the problem reply repeats the typed constraints (G11). A fixture search returns seven records; the appraisal records six claims with exact passages, certainty "low". Design call 1 follows the investigator's stated preference and proposes a single-site case-control study at the tertiary ED on claims c1, c2, c3 and c5 with both gates met on investigator-supplied approvals; it is accepted (ready). Protocol and Stats are completed for that design, and the Analysis stage shows the single site gives only about 62 percent power (about 189 cases against 277 needed). Design call 2 proposes a three-site design with controls matched within site; because Design changed after Protocol and Stats were complete, both are flagged for review (G8). The first decision is not superseded automatically because it was accepted: the investigator withdraws it (withdraw-decision 0), then accepts the second (ready). A reload on the Design route checks that withdrawn, accepted and review required survive. Protocol call 2 carries an outcome with role "co-primary", which must be refused (invalid-enum, then dropped, never demoted to secondary); re-running Protocol and then Stats clears the flags in order. Record ids were computed by the generator with stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts (normalised DOI for records 1, 3, 5 and 7; titleYearKey for records 2, 4 and 6): ev-0gip543, ev-1ggs445, ev-0nr15we, ev-1fmp8sh, ev-0myglbn, ev-0wlu13s, ev-0gln17e. Requires S13 (appraisal path), S11 (selection and action status, withdrawal) and D5 (status text); the refused role and the review flags hold at 875fe59. Catches: an accepted decision silently replaced or erased, two decisions accepted at once, stale downstream stages counted as complete, and an invalid outcome role coerced.

inputs.need:
I am an emergency physician and research lead for three emergency departments in one health region: our tertiary centre and two community hospitals. Since March 2023 our tertiary ED has run a case management program for frequent attenders, defined as eight or more ED visits in 12 months. A social worker or nurse case manager builds a care plan with the patient, their family doctor and community services, and the plan is flagged in the ED record. The two community EDs started the same program in 2024.

The health authority wants to know whether the program should continue. Visit counts are the obvious measure, but frequent attendance tends to fall on its own after a peak, so a simple before-after comparison would flatter the program. What matters more to us is whether enrolled patients are less likely to die or be admitted to intensive care. Deaths and ICU admissions are fairly rare in this group, and working out each patient's exposure to case management means reading the case management files by hand, so I think a matched case-control study is the efficient design: cases are frequent attenders who died or were admitted to ICU, and controls are frequent attenders who did not, matched on age, sex and time.

I would prefer to start at our own ED, where the program has run longest and the files are complete, and add the two community EDs later if needed. We need help with how to match, how to define exposure (ever enrolled, time since enrolment, number of case manager contacts), how to handle the fact that sicker patients are enrolled first, and how many cases we need. The regional ethics board and all three sites have already approved data access. Two research assistants can read files for about 15 hours a week each until June 2027.
inputs.constraints: Two research assistants for about 15 hours a week each until June 2027; file reading must fit that time. No contact with patients or families. Data leave each site only as de-identified extracts under the regional data-sharing agreement. The health authority expects a report by September 2027.

The three emergency departments signed a data-sharing agreement for de-identified extracts on 2026-08-30 (DSA-2026-044).
The tertiary ED's program has enrolled about 420 frequent attenders since March 2023; the two community EDs have enrolled about 230 since 2024.
About 1,900 people a year meet the frequent attender definition across the three EDs, about 1,050 of them at the tertiary ED.
Reading a case management file takes a research assistant about 45 minutes; confirming that a control has no file takes about 15 minutes.

records.title: Case management for frequent emergency department users: a systematic review of effects on visits and costs
records.authors: Harrington-Oyelaran P, Veld-Nakamura S, Castaneda-Boateng R
records.abstract: We identified 31 studies of case management for adults who frequently attend emergency departments, 5 of them randomised trials. Most reported fewer emergency visits after enrolment, but the before-after studies could not separate the programme from regression to the mean, and the randomised trials found smaller reductions (median 12 percent). Only 6 studies reported mortality or intensive care admission, with inconsistent results. Programme content, caseloads and definitions of frequent use varied widely. The authors call for evaluations of hard outcomes that account for regression to the mean.

records.title: Mortality and intensive care admission among frequent emergency department attenders: a regional linkage study
records.abstract: Linking regional emergency department and hospital data for 8,900 adults with eight or more visits in a year, we found 12-month mortality of 3.4 percent and intensive care admission of 2.9 percent, together affecting 6.0 percent of frequent attenders. Risk was highest among those with heart failure, chronic lung disease or alcohol dependence, and among people with no family doctor. Frequent attenders were younger than other patients with the same outcomes. The authors suggest that services for frequent attenders should be judged on these outcomes, not only on visit counts.

records.title: Case management enrolment and 12-month death or intensive care admission in frequent attenders: a matched case-control study at one urban emergency department
records.authors: Nwankwo-Stead L, Bergmann-Achebe T, Iyer-Fontaine C
records.abstract: We identified 64 frequent attenders who died or were admitted to intensive care within 12 months of an index visit and matched four controls to each on age, sex and index month. Case management enrolment before the index date was less common among cases (odds ratio 0.62, 95 percent CI 0.38 to 1.01) after adjustment for prior visits and comorbidity. The estimate was imprecise because of the small number of cases, and enrolment favoured patients with social rather than medical needs. The authors recommend a multi-site study with more cases.

records.title: Confounding by indication in evaluations of case management: enrolment favours the most complex patients
records.abstract: Using data from four case management programmes, we compared patients enrolled with eligible patients not enrolled. Enrolled patients had more emergency visits in the previous year (median 14 against 10), more mental health diagnoses and more housing instability. Without adjustment for these factors, enrolment appeared to double the risk of death; after adjustment for prior visit count and a comorbidity index, the association reversed. The authors recommend matching or adjusting on prior utilisation and measuring exposure only before the outcome date.

records.title: Measuring exposure to case management from care plan files: agreement between two abstractors
records.abstract: Two trained abstractors independently read 150 case management files to record enrolment date, number of case manager contacts and care plan content. Agreement on enrolment date within 14 days was excellent (kappa 0.81), but agreement on the number of contacts was moderate (weighted kappa 0.58) because contacts were recorded in several places. Reading a file took a median of 44 minutes. The authors recommend using enrolment date as the main exposure and treating contact counts as a secondary exposure with a written abstraction guide.

records.title: Variation in frequent attender case management across community and tertiary emergency departments
records.abstract: We compared case management programmes for frequent attenders at 12 emergency departments. Caseloads ranged from 35 to 80 patients per case manager, and community departments more often relied on nurses than social workers. Enrolment criteria differed: 8 departments used a visit threshold alone and 4 added clinical judgement. Median time from eligibility to enrolment was 3 weeks at tertiary and 9 weeks at community departments. The authors suggest that multi-site evaluations match or stratify by site because programme intensity differs.

records.title: Incidence density sampling of controls for time-varying programme exposure
records.abstract: When exposure to a programme changes over time, controls sampled from people who never had the outcome can bias a case-control estimate. We show with simulated data that sampling controls from those still at risk at each case's event date (incidence density sampling) recovers the true rate ratio, whereas sampling from survivors to the end of follow-up overstated a protective effect by up to 30 percent. Exposure must be measured before each matched set's index date. The approach applies directly to enrolment in case management and similar programmes.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Case management reduces visits less than before-after studies suggest, and hard outcomes are rarely evaluated. One single-site case-control study found a protective but imprecise association with death or ICU admission. Confounding by indication can reverse the apparent effect unless prior utilisation and comorbidity are handled, exposure is best measured as enrolment date, controls must be sampled by incidence density, and programme intensity differs between tertiary and community sites. Death or ICU admission affects about 6 percent of frequent attenders a year.
response.gradeRationale: One imprecise case-control study on the outcome of interest and supporting methods evidence; low certainty for any effect on death or ICU admission.

response.reading: Enrolment is not random: the most complex frequent attenders are enrolled first, so a naive comparison makes the program look harmful (claim c2). Death and ICU admission are rare enough that a case-control design is efficient, provided controls are sampled from those still at risk (claim c5) and exposure is measured as enrolment before the index date (claim c3). Programme intensity differs between tertiary and community sites (claim c4), which matters as soon as more than one site is included.

response.designSummary: Conditional logistic regression on within-site matched sets from three emergency departments.
response.sampleSize: At 6 percent a year (claim c6), the tertiary ED gives about 189 cases (March 2023 to December 2025) and the two community EDs about 102 (2024 to 2025), about 291 cases in all. With four controls per case and enrolment in about 21 percent of controls, 291 cases give about 82 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 for an odds ratio of 0.6, against 62 percent for the tertiary ED alone. Site-specific estimates will be imprecise, especially at the community sites, and are reported as secondary.
response.primaryAnalysis: Conditional logistic regression on matched sets (matching within site on age band, sex and calendar month) for enrolment before the index date, adjusted for prior-year visits, comorbidity index, mental health diagnosis, housing instability and family doctor attachment.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Odds ratios by time since enrolment; death alone as a component; site-specific odds ratios with a test of heterogeneity; estimates by family doctor attachment and housing status; contact count as a secondary exposure.
response.missingData: Unavailable files are reported by site; missing housing status is handled by multiple imputation with 20 imputations; a sensitivity analysis excludes matched sets with any unavailable file.
response.multiplicity: One primary association; secondary and site-specific estimates reported with intervals and labelled as secondary.
response.software: R with the survival package; analysis plan filed with the ethics board before abstraction.
overfittingGuards: Five adjustment covariates fixed before abstraction
response.summary: About 291 cases across three sites give about 82 percent power for an odds ratio of 0.6; site estimates are secondary.

steps.note: Re-running Stats clears the last flag: the dependency chain from Design through Protocol to Stats is consistent again (G8).

response.risks: No contact with patients or families. Risks are privacy harm from linking ED, hospital, death and case management data for a stigmatised group, and misuse of findings to cut support; extracts are de-identified at each site and results are reported only in aggregate.
response.consent: Waiver of individual consent for secondary use of records, approved by the regional ethics board; public notice through each hospital's research transparency page.
response.data: Site extracts carry study numbers only; linkage keys stay with the regional data custodian; the analysis file is held on the health authority's research server for seven years.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: frequent attenders include people experiencing homelessness, people with mental illness or addiction, Indigenous people and people without a family doctor. Estimates are reported by family doctor attachment and housing status, community partners review the interpretation, and no subgroup finding is used to exclude people from the program.
response.effectiveness: The study informs whether case management protects against death and ICU admission; a precise null result is a valid answer for the funding review.
response.efficiency: Uses existing records and two research assistants; within-site sampling keeps file reading to about 510 hours.
response.costs: Research assistant time within the approved allocation; data custodian linkage within existing agreements.
response.grants: None needed; a positive result could support an application to evaluate the program's content.
response.partnerships: Case managers at the three sites, the regional data custodian, a community organisation serving people experiencing homelessness, and two people with lived knowledge of frequent ED use as advisors.
response.rebPath: Approved by the regional research ethics board for all three sites on 2026-08-28 (REB-EM-2026-112); data sharing under DSA-2026-044.
response.limitations: Residual confounding by indication; site differences in files; community sites contribute fewer cases.
response.summary: Records-only study with a consent waiver, de-identified site extracts and equity reporting.

response.socialListening: No social media listening; the health authority's patient relations summaries about ED care for frequent attenders are read for themes.

response.title: Case management for frequent emergency department attenders and death or intensive care admission: a three-site matched case-control study
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the association between case management enrolment and death or intensive care admission within 12 months among frequent emergency department attenders. Design: matched case-control study at three emergency departments with incidence density sampling of four controls per case within site. Exposure: enrolment before the index date from case management files. Results will be written after abstraction.
response.introduction: Case management reduces visits less than before-after studies suggest, and its effect on hard outcomes is uncertain; the only case-control estimate came from one site and was imprecise.
response.methods: Cases and controls were drawn from all three sites, with controls matched within site on age band, sex and calendar month. Conditional logistic regression adjusted for complexity. The single-site plan was withdrawn after the sample size calculation showed it was underpowered.
response.results: No data have been abstracted yet. The report will present matched sets by site, exposure distributions, the adjusted odds ratio and site-specific estimates.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh the estimate against confounding by indication and site differences.
response.limitations: Residual confounding; exposure read from files of varying completeness; fewer community cases.
response.summary: STROBE-structured draft; the methods record the withdrawn single-site plan.
